Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment consistent with recurrent transient neurological episodes affecting right hand numbness, arm weakness, leg weakness with gait disturbance lasting several days and increasing in frequency over 1.5-2 months. Associated fatigue and mild nausea reported.  
- Family history significant for carotid artery disease and stroke.  
- Differential includes:  
  • Transient Ischemic Attacks (TIAs) / Mini-strokes – High likelihood due to episodic focal neurological symptoms, family history, and physician’s urgent referral for TIA clinic assessment. Note episodes last several days, longer than classic TIAs.  
  • Multiple Sclerosis (MS) – Moderate likelihood given relapsing-remitting neurological deficits and young adult age, but no specific visual or speech symptoms reported and no objective neurological exam findings documented.  
  • Peripheral nerve entrapment / cervical radiculopathy – Low to medium likelihood; does not fully explain leg symptoms and systemic features.  
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency / metabolic neuropathy – Low likelihood; symptoms episodic, no supporting systemic features or risk factors.  
- Physician’s working diagnosis and management focus on excluding TIA and stroke through urgent referral and investigations.  

Management Plan
- Urgent referral to TIA/ministroke clinic for assessment including carotid artery ultrasound and brain imaging.  
- Patient advised to attend emergency department if symptoms become prolonged or persistent, to exclude stroke.  
- Provided contact numbers for hospital and clinic to ensure timely appointment.  
- Continue monitoring symptoms and liaise with medical services as needed.  
- Aspirin use self-initiated without medical advice; risks and benefits not discussed with GP previously. No change documented to aspirin management.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Transient Ischemic Attacks (TIAs) / Mini-strokes – High likelihood  
  Justification: Recurrent transient unilateral neurological symptoms involving hand, arm, leg with gait abnormalities; strong family history; physician concern and urgent TIA referral align with this diagnosis.  
  Opposed by: Longer episode duration than typical TIAs; young age without classic vascular risk factors.  

- Multiple Sclerosis (MS) – Moderate likelihood  
  Justification: Episodic neurological sensory and motor deficits lasting days, age consistent; fatigue present.  
  Opposed by: No vision or speech symptoms; family history favors vascular cause; no documented neurologic signs on exam.  

- Peripheral nerve entrapment / cervical radiculopathy – Low to moderate likelihood  
  Justification: Unilateral hand symptoms intermittent; however, leg and gait symptoms less explained by this.  

- Vitamin B12 deficiency or metabolic neuropathy – Low likelihood  
  Justification: Sensory/motor symptoms present but episodic nature and lack of other systemic symptoms inconsistent.
